clinicalPearls: An X-linked disorder in which affected males typically have moderate to severe intellectual disability while carrier females are more mildly and variably affected
Characteristic coarse facial features include a prominent forehead, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, a broad nose and full lips with a thick everted lower lip
The hands are distinctive, with soft, fleshy, tapering fingers and lax skin
Skeletal features include short stature, pectus deformity and progressive kyphoscoliosis
Stimulus-induced drop episodes (unexpected sound or tactile stimulus causing a brief collapse without loss of consciousness) are a recognised, non-epileptic feature
Caused by loss-of-function variants in RPS6KA3, encoding the growth-factor-regulated kinase RSK2, with de novo variants common
Progressive hearing loss and cardiac involvement may develop over time
reference.pathophysiology: RPS6KA3 encodes RSK2, a ribosomal S6 kinase that acts as a downstream effector of the Ras-MAPK signalling cascade, phosphorylating transcription factors and other substrates that regulate cell growth, differentiation and, importantly, neuronal function and skeletal development. Loss-of-function variants abolish or reduce kinase activity, impairing signalling required for normal cortical development and bone modelling. Because the gene is X-linked, males with a single affected allele are more severely affected, while females show variable expression influenced by X-inactivation. The disrupted signalling produces the intellectual disability, characteristic facies and progressive skeletal changes.
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey and spine imaging for kyphoscoliosis and pectus deformity
Echocardiography and ECG for cardiac involvement
Audiological assessment for progressive hearing loss
Brain MRI and EEG when seizures or drop episodes occur
Targeted RPS6KA3 sequencing or an intellectual-disability gene panel or exome sequencing
redFlags: Cardiac involvement such as valve disease or arrhythmia
Recurrent stimulus-induced drop attacks causing injury
reference.prognosis: Affected males usually have significant lifelong intellectual disability with progressive skeletal and sometimes cardiac complications; carrier females range from unaffected to mildly impaired. Care is supportive with orthopaedic, cardiac and audiological surveillance.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting stimulus-induced drop attacks as epileptic seizures and over-treating with antiseizure drugs
Overlooking milder cognitive and facial features in carrier females
Failing to monitor for progressive scoliosis and cardiac disease
Attributing the coarse facies to a storage disorder without genetic testing
management: No disease-specific treatment exists; management is supportive and multidisciplinary, centred on developmental and educational support with speech and language therapy, physiotherapy and occupational therapy

Manage stimulus-induced drop episodes by minimising sudden auditory and tactile triggers, with trials of clonazepam, sodium valproate or a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and measures to prevent fall injury
Orthopaedic surveillance and treatment of progressive kyphoscoliosis and pectus deformity, including bracing or surgery
Cardiac surveillance with echocardiography and ECG for valvular disease, particularly mitral involvement
Audiological monitoring and hearing aids for progressive sensorineural hearing loss
Anticonvulsants and EEG-guided management where epileptic seizures occur
Genetic counselling for this X-linked RPS6KA3 disorder, with carrier testing for female relatives and prenatal options; de novo variants are common
